newsitem.title: INDIA: INDIA ORDERS PROBE IN OILFIELDS AWARDS.
newsitem.headline: INDIA ORDERS PROBE IN OILFIELDS AWARDS.

text.p: India said on Friday it has initiated an inquiry into the manner in which drilling contracts for three discovered offshore oilfields were awarded to private-sector oil firms.

T.R. Baalu, the junior petroleum minister, told the upper house of parliament that a "preliminary inquiry" has been started by the federal Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) into the contracts for the Panna and Mukta oilfields in western India and the Ravva oilfield in southwestern India.
The Panna and Mukta fields were awarded to a joint venture of Enron Oil & Gas India Ltd, an affiliate of U.S. multinational Enron Oil and Gas Co and India's Reliance Industries Ltd in October 1994.
The Ravva contract went to a consortium comprising Videocon Petroleum Ltd, a unit of Videocon International Ltd, Cairn Energy Plc's Australian unit Command Petroleum Ltd and Japan's Marubeni Corp.

A Petroleum Ministry official, who requested anonymity, told Reuters the CBI enquiry was ordered to establish why state-run Oil and Natural Gas Corp was not compensated for the costs incurred in developing the fields.
Officials of the private firms were not immediately available for comment.
Petroleum Minister Janeshwar Mishra said India's Comptroller and Auditor-General had in a report commented on the ONGC costs issue.

"CAG in their final report...of 1996 on participation of private parties with ONGC in production of crude oil and natural gas made observations relating to non-reimbursement of past costs to ONGC, bid evaluation criteria, non-opening of bids in public, (and) reserve variation of Panna-Mukta oil field," Mishra said.

The Petroleum Ministry official said the CBI inquiry "will also look into the allegation that ONGC officials negotiating the contracts were given high positions by the companies in return for favours".
However Baalu said the government had no intention to review the contracts it had awarded for the fields.
"The contracts for development of discovered fields have been signed in pursuance of government policy and there is no proposal to cancel these contracts," he said.
Last month the Videocon-Command-Marubeni consortium said the Ravva oil and gas project would have a positive cash flow by the fourth quarter of 1998.

The Ravva field started producing crude in November 1996 after the consortium took it over from ONGC in January 1994. It produces between 38,000 and 39,000 barrels of crude per day or about five percent of India's total production. It also produces a million cubic metres of natural gas per day.
The Panna and Mukta fields are part of the Bombay Offshore basin in western India. Enron Oil and Gas India Ltd and Reliance signed the contract to drill for oil in the two fields in December 1994.
Mishra said ONGC has a 40 percent participating interest in the Panna-Mukta production-sharing contract (PSC).
